processing: Shui Xian leaf made in the rock-oolong way: partly oxidised, rolled, then roasted, often in more than one round.
harvest_season: As with other Wuyi rock teas, a single spring picking.
appearance_dry: Long, dark twisted strips typical of Shui Xian.
appearance_wet: Large leaves with darkened edges, typical of the cultivar.
taste_profile: Typical Shui Xian is orchid-scented with a high, long aroma, and old bushes from rocky sites are held to be better; the core valleys are prized for the strongest rock character.

brewing.notes: Near-boiling water and short steeps; good rock tea should hold over many infusions.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually after the roast has rested, and Shui Xian is known to keep well, so older lots appear too. Valley names are easily borrowed, so expect a premium and ask for evidence of the site.
description:
This is Shui Xian, the big-leaved Wuyi staple, from one particular address: Huiyuan Keng, one of the valleys in the group known as San Keng Liang Jian, the three pits and two streams regarded as the heart of rock tea.

The site is the point. A keng is a hollow enclosed by slopes, which holds humidity and evens out day and night temperatures, and that microclimate is credited with the difference in flavour. The making itself follows the usual rock-oolong route.

Little has been written about the tasting character of this one valley's Shui Xian. As a guide, Shui Xian in general is orchid-scented, and old bushes from rocky sites are held to be better. Brew hot and quick and let it run through many steeps.

The appellation is what you are paying for and what is easiest to fake. Buy from someone who can name the plot and the year, and compare it against a plainer Wuyi Shui Xian.
history: Huiyuan Keng is named among the classic core valleys of Wuyi rock tea, and Shui Xian is one of the region's main cultivars. No separate history of this valley's Shui Xian as a named tea is documented.
